\section[\hi{जनवरी} \hi{फ़रवरी} \hi{मार्च} \hi{अप्रैल} \hi{मई} \hi{जून} \hi{जुलाई} \hi{अगस्त} \hi{सितंबर} \hi{अक्टूबर} \hi{नवंबर} \hi{दिसंबर}]{\hi{जनवरी} to \hi{दिसंबर} — borrowed names, and a second calendar underneath}

\label{lesson:HI-C16-mahine}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Warm-up.} {[}PAUSE 2s{]} Like Arabic, Hindi doesn't have just \textbf{one} set of months — everyday civil life and traditional/religious life run on \textbf{two different calendars}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The Gregorian months — recent, borrowed}
For dates, school, business, and government, Hindi uses month names borrowed straightforwardly from \textbf{English}:

\textbf{\hi{जनवरी}, \hi{फ़रवरी}, \hi{मार्च}, \hi{अप्रैल}, \hi{मई}, \hi{जून}, \hi{जुलाई}, \hi{अगस्त}, \hi{सितंबर}, \hi{अक्टूबर}, \hi{नवंबर}, \hi{दिसंबर}} (\emph{janvarī, farvarī, mārc, aprail, maī, jūn, julāī, agast, sitambar, aktūbar, navambar, disambar}) — you can hear "January," "March," "August" right through the Hindi pronunciation. This is a modern civil borrowing, not an ancient Sanskrit system.

\subsection*{You'll want to know — Be honest: the traditional calendar is a genuinely different structure}
Hindu tradition keeps its \textbf{own}, much older lunisolar calendar — \textbf{\hi{विक्रम} \hi{संवत्}} (\emph{Vikram Samvat}) — with twelve \textbf{different} month names: \textbf{\hi{चैत्र}, \hi{वैशाख}, \hi{ज्येष्ठ}, \hi{आषाढ़}, \hi{श्रावण}, \hi{भाद्रपद}, \hi{आश्विन}, \hi{कार्तिक}, \hi{मार्गशीर्ष}, \hi{पौष}, \hi{माघ}, \hi{फाल्गुन}} (\emph{Chaitra, Vaiśākh, Jyeṣṭha, Āṣāḍh, Śrāvaṇ, Bhādrapad, Āśvin, Kārtik, Mārgaśīrṣ, Pauṣ, Māgh, Phālgun}).

This isn't just a second set of labels for the same twelve solar months — these months are tied to the \textbf{six-ṛtu} seasonal calendar from the seasons lesson (in the traditional/classical scheme, each pair of Vikram Samvat months corresponds to one of the six \emph{ṛtu}), and major festivals (Holi, Diwali, and many others) are dated by \textbf{this} calendar, not the Gregorian one — which is why their Gregorian-calendar date shifts from year to year.

\subsection*{Guided Practice}
{[}PAUSE 1s{]}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item {[}YOU SAY: "janvarī, mārc, agast" — hear the borrowed English names{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the traditional calendar — "Chaitra, Vaiśākh, Jyeṣṭha"{]}
  \item {[}YOU SAY: the honest point — festivals shift on the Gregorian calendar because they're dated by Vikram Samvat instead{]}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Wrap-up recall}]
{[}PAUSE 3s{]} Where do Hindi's everyday civil month names come from? (\textbf{Borrowed from English} — \emph{janvarī, mārc, agast}...) What traditional calendar runs alongside it, and what is it tied to? (\textbf{Vikram Samvat} — tied to the \textbf{six ṛtu} seasons, not the four-season Western frame.) Why do festivals like Holi and Diwali fall on different Gregorian dates each year? (\textbf{They're dated by Vikram Samvat}, a different calendar system entirely.)
\end{tcolorbox}
